full_judgment:
"It is stated that there has been considerable change in the Policy of the Government in prohibiting consumption of alcoholic beverage in 1950 the Government introduced prohibition under which numbers of liquor shops where reduced and Muslims were debarred lion drinking alcoholic liquor on medical ground. After liberation the measures were further tightened as such so that the number of liquor shops were further reduced and Muslims were completely debarred from taking liquor even on medical grounds. In the wake of these prohibitive measures people were found using increasingly Mritasanjibani as beverage which posed as a potential danger to the national health and ran counter to the Government policy. This necessitated the amendment of the Rule in question which the Government is competent to make under the provision of the law force and without destroying the Ayurvedic components and properties of said medicines." 

 22. In addition to the powers of (he Govt. to regulate the manufacture and consumption of liquor under these provisions of the Act itself as mentioned above, the Government did, in exercise of the powers conferred by sections 4, 5, 19(4), 85 and 86 of the Excise Act, made certain rules known. as the Excise (Foreign and Country Liquor Prohibition and Restriction) Rules, 1950, briefly called the Prohibition Rules. These Rules set out in detail the various measures in relation to prohibitions. There is neither an ambiguity nor vagueness as to the effect to be achieved by these Rules. Of these Rules, Rule 2(9), defines "medicated wine" as meaning wines or spirit compounded with various drugs and includes & Carely Ltd., (1952) A C 427 at page 450", capable of being related to one of the prescribed purposes and it can; therefore, be challenged as being outside the powers of the rule-making authority . Having referred to one of the purpose of the Act and the effect intended by the Rules of 1936 which were framed in order to achieve that purpose, it is obvious that the Rules (of 1936) which contained Rule 15 were made in accordance with and authorised by the words of delegation as occur in sections 85 and 86(2) of the Act, the primary consideration in making the Rules seem to be the concern for preserving and maintaining the medicinal quality of these preparations. From the presence of the distinction between liquor or intoxicating drug and medicinal preparations which may contain alcoholic spirit, which is clearly discernible from the language employed in the Act itself and the objects and purpose in making and promulgating two sets of Rules which clearly preserved the distinction, there can be no confusion as regards the limits of the rule-making authority. Proceeding on the assumption that Mritasanjibani Sura/ Sudha are Mritasanjibani, Sura or Sudha.
